title: Uzbek — official Latin alphabet (1995)
authority: Law of 2 Sept 1993 as amended 6 May 1995; Orthographic Rules, Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 339 of 24 Aug 1995
description: Uzbek Cyrillic converted to the official Uzbek Latin alphabet: Ў→oʻ, Ғ→gʻ (U+02BB), Қ→q, Ҳ→h, Х→x, Ж→j, Ъ→tutuq ʼ (U+02BC), Ь omitted, Е→ye initially and after vowels, Ц→ts after vowels and s elsewhere.
notes: 2026 reform: a law replacing Oʻ→Ö, Gʻ→Ğ, Sh→Ş, Ch→Ç (28 letters + apostrophe) passed the Legislative Chamber (July 2026) and the Senate (10 Sept 2026); presidential signature was unconfirmed as of 7 Oct 2026. Documents in the current alphabet stay valid; schools switch from 2027, textbooks by 2031. This scheme keeps the 1995 alphabet.
Code points: oʻ and gʻ use U+02BB, the tutuq uses U+02BC, as prescribed; much real-world text (including government sites) uses U+2018, U+2019 or U+0027 instead.
ICAO Doc 9303 §6.B maps U+040E Ў to U (the Belarusian letter). In Uzbek the same code point is oʻ, so Ўринов → Oʻrinov here, not Urinov.

Context rules from the orthography as summarised by Wikipedia: Е→ye word-initially and after a vowel (and after ъ/ь); Ц→ts after a vowel, otherwise s; Ь omitted but ьи/ьо → yi/yo; no tutuq after oʻ (мўъжиза → moʻjiza); s+h is split with a tutuq (Исҳоқ → Isʼhoq). The rules were not checked word by word against the lex.uz text.
Щ and Ы are not Uzbek letters; Russian names containing them are rendered shch and i (Быков → Bikov) as in Uzbek usage.
BGN/PCGN 2000 (uz_bgn_pcgn) differs only in details: Ц always ts, Ь→’, apostrophes U+2018/U+2019.

rules.note: tutuq separates s+h from the digraph sh (Исҳоқ → Isʼhoq)
no tutuq after oʻ: мўъжиза → moʻjiza
